title: POC scoping: cost modeling with Auriga Systems
summary: Auriga wants a 6-week pilot to validate latency and unit economics for an LLM-powered code-assist feature. Primary success criteria: sub-250ms median token latency for interactive flows, cost <= $0.03 per user request at expected QPS, integration with SSO and KMS. Redwood to run benchmarks (hosted + dedicated) and provide per-token estimates plus batching/caching config. Security docs and pilot SOW to be shared.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and initial per-token cost model (Samir) - due 2026-03-20
Auriga to provide production sample workload traces and a 7-day request sample (Priya) - due 2026-03-22
Schedule 90-minute benchmark run with Auriga test data (Lina) - tentatively 2026-03-26
Send pilot SOW and pricing options (hosted vs dedicated) (Samir) - due 2026-03-23
action_items: Samir: Share initial cost model spreadsheet and README (due 2026-03-20)
Lina: Prepare benchmark scripts and runbook for Auriga (due 2026-03-24)
Priya: Export and share 7-day sample of request traces + typical prompt lengths (due 2026-03-22)
Sara: Send list of required compliance docs (SOC2 scope, KMS, encryption-at-rest) (due 2026-03-21)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel, Lina Gomez, Ethan Wu (Redwood) — Mark Reynolds, Priya Singh, Ben Carter, Sara Kim (Auriga)
Shared links: https://redwood.ai/s/auriga-poc-benchmarks, SOW draft (will share)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Samir from Redwood, that's lina and ethan with me. hows everybody doing?
[00:06] Mark: good thanks, bit of a weird afternoon but we're all set.
[00:12] Priya: yes thanks, excited to get into the cost modeling piece.
[00:18] Samir: cool quick agenda — we want to align on your success criteria, get the workload sizing, agree benchmark plan and timelines, then we'll talk unit economics (per-token), batching and caching knobs, and pilot scope. sound ok?
[00:29] Ben: yep that works. high level our goal is to add a contextual code assist inside our IDE product, low latency is critical, and cost needs to hit our unit economics target — we have a budget for the pilot roughly 25k USD for the initial 6 weeks.
[00:44] Lina: great, can you walk through expected QPS and typical prompt/response lengths? even rough numbers help a lot.
[00:52] Priya: sure — for the pilot we expect 100 concurrent developers hitting the feature, peak QPS around 40-60 requests per second. typical prompt is 120 tokens, average generated response 180 tokens. but there's a heavy tail, some requests go 800+ tokens during larger refactors.
[01:15] Ethan: and are prompts mostly unique or do you have repetitive prefixes? e.g. repo context that could be cached?
[01:23] Priya: good question — there is a lot of repeated context, we send file headers and repo metadata frequently. so prefix caching could help, maybe 20-35% token reuse?
[01:35] Samir: perfect that's actually a big lever. if we can cache the repo prefix and reuse KV, effective token count for generation drops considerably. that impacts per-request cost.
[01:44] Mark: on security — we need SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS integration for keys. also data residency in the EU for some customers, so private or VPC deployment may be needed.
[01:57] Lina: we support SAML, RBAC, and can integrate with customer KMS. for residency dedicated/private deployments are the route; hosted API can also be done via region controls but for strict residency we usually recommend Private.
[02:10] Ben: what's the rough delta in unit cost between hosted and dedicated?
[02:15] Samir: depends on throughput. for small pilots hosted is simplest — our per-token price we quote to customers typically is model-dependent. for example (ballpark numbers) a 13B dense model on hosted might be $0.0006 per input token and $0.0012 per output token billed; but your true cost depends on batching, caching and sequence lengths. with dedicated and reserved capacity the per-token infra cost can drop 30-50% at scale because of higher GPU utilization; but there's a monthly committed capacity fee.
[02:48] Priya: ok but we need to map to our target: we want per-user request cost <= $0.003 after batching and caching at pilot loads.
[02:57] Samir: right, let's run numbers. given your average request of 300 tokens total (120 input + 180 output) naive hosted bill would be ~ (120*0.0006 + 180*0.0012) = 0.072 + 0.216 = $0.288?? wait that's off, sorry, that's my bad math, hang on.
[03:17] Ethan: (laughs) transcription note — quick sanity check.
[03:20] Samir: sorry mixing units — should be 120 * 0.0006 = 0.072 — oh that's cents, yes 0.072 USD, 180 * 0.0012 = 0.216 USD, so total ~0.288 USD per request — you're right that's way too high for interactive. that indicates model choice matters a lot. if we use a smaller quantized model or better batching the per-token compute price drops.
[03:44] Priya: 0.288 is above our target obviously. what options do we have?
[03:49] Lina: options — 1) choose a smaller but high quality model (7B quantized, or LLAMA-like 7B quant) which reduces per-token compute cost; 2) enable prefix/KV caching to cut input tokens by 20-40%; 3) use continuous batching to increase GPU utilization (batch windows), 4) use Redwood Dedicated with reserved capacity to reduce infra per-token cost, and 5) apply sequence-length trimming heuristics for long tail requests.
[04:12] Ben: how much does caching typically save in practice? you said 20-35% reuse earlier.
[04:17] Lina: yes in our experience caching typical for repo-based prompts can reduce net input tokens by ~25-45% depending on how much context is static. that means if your average 120 input tokens has 40% static context, you only pay compute on 72 new tokens effectively.
[04:33] Samir: also batching — if we can accept a 20-50ms extra latency tail we can batch small requests and improve GPU utilization; that often reduces per-token infra cost by 15-30% in practice. combined with caching you can get to delta that meets your $0.03 target.
[04:49] Priya: can you show the model/recommendation tradeoffs? like expected per-request cost for a 7B quant vs 13B quant vs 70B hosted?
[04:58] Samir: yes we'll put a modeled table in the spreadsheet. rough quick numbers — 7B quant hosted: input token $0.00015, output $0.0003; 13B quant: input $0.0003, output $0.0006; 70B dense: input $0.0009, output $0.0018 — again very approximate. So for your 300 token request at 7B quant naive: 120*0.00015 + 180*0.0003 = 0.018 + 0.054 = 0.072 USD per request — still ~7 cents, which is 0.072 USD, that's above $0.03 but we're not yet applying caching/batching and billing granularity.
[05:38] Ethan: i want to flag that some vendors bill per 1k tokens or have different input/output multipliers; the spreadsheet will show per-1k numbers to avoid confusion.
[05:48] Mark: we need to be below $0.003 per request, which is about 0.3 cents. seems like a big gap. are we misunderstanding the metric? maybe per-user per-day rather than per-request?
[06:01] Priya: good point — our internal metric is cost per successful assist, which averages 3 requests per developer per day, so budget per request target is indeed low; maybe we mean 0.03? hmm i'll check. (pause) ok confirm — it's actually $0.03 per request target, not $0.003. my mistake.
[06:23] Samir: great that's helpful — $0.03 per request target. so we need to get from e.g., naive 7B quant 0.072 -> 0.03. achievable with caching (40% reduction) and batching/reserved capacity. let's run hypothetical: 0.072 * (1 - 0.40 caching) = 0.043; then with dedicated utilization improvements maybe 30% infra saving -> 0.030ish. that lines up.
[06:47] Ben: ok good. what's the pilot timeline look like? we asked for a 6-week pilot.
[06:53] Lina: here's a proposed schedule: week 0 (this week) align on success criteria, obtain trace data; week 1 run baseline host benchmarks with sample traces; week 2 run dedicated benchmark and caching experiments; week 3 iterate on prompt engineering and batching windows; week 4 run stability and scaling tests; week 5 refine cost model and produce final report; week 6 wrap up and discuss production roll plan.
[07:14] Priya: that seems solid. what do you need from us to start?
[07:18] Samir: sample traces (7-day), list of tenant/residency needs, SSO and KMS contacts, and a PO for the pilot if you want Redwood to provision dedicated nodes. For hosted pilot we can start without PO.
[07:30] Priya: we'll send traces. also need to know expected artifact from Redwood — final report, cost model, recommended config, and SOW?
[07:38] Samir: yes deliverables: benchmark repo + run results, per-token cost model (spreadsheet), recommended batching/caching config, and pilot SOW with pricing options (hosted vs dedicated) and next steps for production.
[07:49] Sara: on compliance — we need SOC2 evidence, encryption at rest details, HSM/KMS integration details, and audit-log retention options.
[07:59] Lina: we'll share the security pack, and for KMS we have examples of both customer-managed and Redwood-managed keyflows. note: for private deployments we can do customer KMS in the VPC.
[08:12] Mark: benchmarks — how reproducible are latency numbers? we care about median and p95 under realistic tail.
[08:19] Ethan: we record median, p95, p99 and cost per 1k tokens. for interactive flows we optimize for median < 250ms and p95 < 700ms as typical targets on dedicated infra; hosted numbers differ by region and model. we will run load-gen with your traces to reproduce tails.
[08:36] Ben: can you run an initial smoke test with our smallest sample to show ballpark numbers?
[08:41] Lina: yes that's in scope — once we get traces we can run a 1-hour smoke and share initial per-request cost and latency.
[08:49] Priya: what about quantization and accuracy regressions? we can't sacrifice developer experience.
[08:55] Samir: good call. part of the POC is quality evals — we'll run evals on your prompt set to compare outputs across models (7B quant vs 13B quant) and flag regressions. you get quality metrics alongside cost.
[09:07] Mark: any surprises or typical gotchas we should watch for?
[09:11] Ethan: watch out for long context requests — KV cache helps, but if users paste full repo files it's heavy. also multi-turn stateful conversations increase KV size. batching windows that are too wide can add latency spikes. and data egress/residency for EU customers can add infra constraints/cost.
[09:29] Priya: on budget — we have $25k for pilot; how far does that go on dedicated nodes?
[09:35] Samir: depends on node type and model; for example a single A10G or H100-equivalent pool for a small dedicated pilot might run $8k-$12k/month depending on commit and region. for 6 weeks that's ~12k-18k. plus Redwood platform/premium support fees. we can propose a slim dedicated config to fit $25k including run costs and engineering support.
[09:56] Ben: decision criteria for production — besides cost/latency we need ops readiness: observability, per-route dashboards, rollback and model pinning.
[10:06] Lina: all part of Redwood Console — we'll include dashboards and tracing hooks in the final report; rollouts and fallback policies are supported.
[10:14] Samir: okay last bit — benchmarks we'll publish in the shared spreadsheet, and we'll give you per-1k token and per-request modeled columns plus sensitivity to caching %, batching window ms, and model choice.
[10:26] Priya: sounds good. please include an A/B test suggestion for canary rollout to prod.
[10:31] Samir: will do.
[10:33] Mark: cool any final questions?
[10:36] Priya: none here. thanks team.
[10:38] Samir: thanks everyone. recap: samir shares cost model + spreadsheet by 3/20, auriga shares traces by 3/22, schedule benchmark run 3/26. action items in the notes.
[10:50] (call ends)
